The Sky emperor (Lethrinus mahsena) is a commercially valued lethrinid species distributed across the coral reefs of the Indo-West Pacific region. Studies examining maximum body size from extensive fishery-independent surveys indicate that individuals can attain a fork length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters], representing the largest recorded specimens from unfished populations. This asymptotic size is consistent with the moderate growth rates and extended longevity typical of many tropical lethrinids inhabiting stable reef environments. In contrast, the onset of sexual maturation occurs considerably earlier in the life history, with gonadal development initiating when fish reach a fork length of 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters]. This pubertal length threshold corresponds to roughly thirty percent of the ultimate fork length, a proportion that aligns with expectations for iteroparous reef fishes that allocate substantial resources to somatic growth before shifting investment toward reproductive tissues. The relatively early maturation relative to maximum size may reflect selective pressures imposed by natural mortality rates in the predator-rich reef habitat.

Spawning activity in Lethrinus mahsena has been investigated through both direct observation of gravid females on the reef and through histological examination of gonadal tissue across seasonal sampling periods. Under the thermal conditions typical of spawning aggregations in the central Indian Ocean during peak reproductive months (23 °C [T = 23 °C]), females produce approximately 227,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 227,000 eggs per year]. No separate clutch size or spawning frequency estimates are available, so the daily reproductive rate is inferred directly from the annual egg production figure, yielding an average of around 622 eggs per day under those thermal conditions. The choice of 23 °C as a reference temperature reflects the mean thermal regime experienced by spawning aggregations. Temperature is known to influence vitellogenic rates and oocyte development duration in tropical teleosts, and the reported fecundity value should be interpreted within the context of this specific environmental condition.

An unusually precise estimate of neonatal mass is available for this species, derived from the measured egg diameter of 0.335 millimeters. Using the geometric relationship for a sphere, the calculated wet weight at birth is 2 × 10⁻⁵ grams [Wwb = 2 × 10⁻⁵ grams], a minute initial body size that characterizes the pelagic larval phase common to most lethrinids. This extremely small birth mass has profound implications for larval ecology, as the newly hatched larvae possess limited endogenous yolk reserves and must rapidly acquire exogenous feeding skills to avoid starvation during the critical first-feeding window. The planktonic larvae drift in the water column for weeks, undergoing substantial morphological transformations before settling to the benthos. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest that this birth mass is typical of Lethrinus, which produce large numbers of small pelagic eggs rather than a smaller number of well-provisioned demersal eggs. The small initial size also implies high natural mortality rates during the early larval stages, a common demographic bottleneck among marine reef fishes with pelagic larval dispersal.

Longevity records for Lethrinus mahsena have been assembled from otolith-based age determinations across multiple geographic regions, providing robust estimates of maximum lifespan. The oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of 27 years [am = 27 years] when inhabiting waters with an average temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a thermal regime characteristic of the equatorial reefs where this species is most abundant. This lifespan is among the more extended values reported for tropical lethrinids, likely reflecting the relatively low natural mortality rates and stable environmental conditions in unfished or lightly exploited populations. The 28 °C temperature is significant because metabolic rates, somatic growth, and senescence processes are all temperature-dependent in ectotherms; cooler thermal regimes would be expected to prolong lifespan further, while warmer conditions might accelerate aging. The combination of a 27-year maximum lifespan (27 years) [am = 27 years] and a moderate asymptotic length of 65 centimeters [Li = 65 centimeters] suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic persistence and repeated reproductive events over rapid turnover at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Understanding the demographic resilience of Lethrinus mahsena requires integrating these life-history parameters into a coherent demographic framework. Individuals that survive the pelagic larval bottleneck, hatching with an initial body mass of only 2 × 10⁻⁵ grams [Wwb = 2 × 10⁻⁵ grams], face an extended juvenile period before entering the adult population. The attainment of sexual maturation at 19 centimeters [Lp = 19 centimeters] fork length represents a major life-history transition, after which fish begin allocating a portion of their acquired energy toward gamete production. A female's annual egg output of approximately 227,000 eggs [Ri = annual egg output of approximately 227,000 eggs] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], when viewed alongside the species' documented longevity of 27 years [am = 27 years] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], implies a lifetime reproductive output that can exceed several million eggs under favorable conditions. However, the vast majority of these offspring perish during the early larval phase, and only a tiny fraction will survive to recruit into the adult population and ultimately reach the 65-centimeter maximum fork length (65 centimeters) [Li = 65 centimeters] recorded for the species. This high fecundity but low juvenile survival is a classic demographic strategy among marine fishes with pelagic larval dispersal.
